chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb, from ʿAlī ibn al-Sindī, from Ḥammād, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام about a man who is an Imam and begins with al-Ḥamd, and does not say, “Bismi llāhi al-Raḥmāni al-Raḥīmi.” He said: “It does not harm him, and there is no problem in that.”

So the proper way to understand this report is the state of taqiyyah, as we have explained, because along with taqiyyah it is permissible to recite it quietly, as we have previously discussed. And it is also possible that the report concerns one who did not say that out of forgetfulness, not that it occurred from him deliberately.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation or precautionary concealment in circumstances of risk
key_terms.بِالْحَمْدِ: with Sūrat al-Ḥamd, the opening chapter recited in salat (prayer)
key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ: the basmalah formula at the opening of the surah
key_terms.لَا يَضُرُّهُ: it does not invalidate or harm him
key_terms.نَاسِيًا: having omitted it out of forgetfulness

ai.seo_question: What does Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām say about an Imam who omits Bismi llāhi al-Raḥmāni al-Raḥīmi in salat (prayer)?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling on an Imam in salat (prayer) who begins Sūrat al-Ḥamd without reciting “Bismi llāhi al-Raḥmāni al-Raḥīmi.” The apparent allowance is explained in light of taqiyyah or forgetfulness, indicating a juristic reconciliation of the narration within the broader rulings of prayer recitation.
